The Last Word

01 · Before you listen

A few words to know

Explore the vocabulary
reconcile
Compare records to explain any differences.
attribution
The assignment of an act to a particular person.
contemporaneous
Created at the time an event occurred.
discrepancy
A difference that requires explanation.
enduring
Lasting for a long time.
conspicuous
Easy to notice or prominently visible.

04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Fiona Bell's call the following morning began with a sentence Emma had spent weeks hoping to hear: the bank had located the transaction behind the matching follow-up reference. An independent accountant had compared its surviving record with the recovered authorisations book and the trust's exception register.

The original transfer had been returned. A subsequent payment, carrying the same follow-up reference, had gone into an account controlled by the Glenarraidh Education Trust. The exception was nevertheless marked resolved. There was no verified onward transfer to the intended student among the records examined.

“Then we have proof the grant was stolen,” Sarah said.

“We have proof that the recorded destination was the trust's account,” Emma replied. “That's serious enough to investigate. It isn't proof of what happened afterwards, or of anyone's criminal intention.”

The independent review had also identified a signed authorisation sheet attached to that exception. Malcolm Vale's full name appeared beneath the approval, and the signature had been checked against contemporaneous signed trust documents. Unlike the blurred initials that had tempted them earlier, this was evidence supporting attribution of one specific decision. It did not transform every other manual entry into Malcolm's act, nor establish that he had received the money personally.

Emma could already see the report she would write: an exception closed administratively without evidence, in the material examined, that the intended recipient had received the grant. The discrepancy demanded an explanation and a wider audit. It did not entitle her to invent one.

Then Fiona disclosed the evidence that changed Emma's understanding of the letters. Among the trust's 2026 correspondence was an email from Malcolm's work account containing the complete wording of the later warning sent in Claire Morrison's name. It instructed a colleague to arrange delivery as though Claire were its author. Emma and Sarah checked the original electronic record against courier documentation and the letter Emma had kept. Both the wording and the delivery trail matched.

They contacted Malcolm before publication. Confronted with the records, he acknowledged arranging the second letter and said his intention had been to stop a distressing investigation. He maintained that the travel scheme's accounts had innocent explanations and denied taking students' money. Emma preserved his response in full. A documented act of impersonation was not, by itself, a finding of financial fraud.

That evening Fiona offered something the registers never could: contact with the woman whose disappearance had begun the story. Claire had agreed to a private video conversation, provided her present location remained confidential.

At first Emma saw only the reflection of a lamp in the screen. Then Claire appeared, older, tired around the eyes, unmistakably herself and yet a person Emma could no longer pretend to know. The two women checked the draft and courier booking for the first letter, written on 14 October 2026 and delivered the following day. James Morrison privately confirmed details of their shared past. Emma would neither disclose those details nor turn them into a trail towards Claire's home.

“I sent the first letter,” Claire said. “I didn't send the warning.”

She described the days after their interview on 18 September 2011. She had questioned the way the trust reported support for students, concerned that approval and actual payment were being spoken of as though they were identical. She said she had felt threatened, not because she possessed proof of wholesale theft, but because her questions made powerful people angry and seemed to put her brother and the students at risk. Her fears were part of her testimony, not independently established facts about every person she suspected.

On 21 September, Daniel Reid had helped her leave Glenarraidh. He had driven her away from the village; he had not abducted her, and he did not know where she lived now. Nora's old account of Claire entering a car voluntarily was therefore compatible with Claire's own description of the pressure she had felt.

“People kept asking whether I chose to leave,” Claire told Emma. “I did. Nobody asked what I thought would happen if I stayed.”

Emma remembered the headline she had written after the disappearance, suggesting that Claire had left over a personal dispute. She had been young and ambitious; neither fact excused presenting a poorly sourced interpretation as an answer. James had been right to resent it.

“I published the wrong story,” Emma said. “And I made your family live with it.”

“Then publish what you can prove,” Claire replied. “Keep my address out of it. I'll decide when and how to speak to James.”

Emma agreed. She did not ask where Claire lived. Having finally heard from her, she understood that access was not ownership.

The article appeared the following day. It documented the returned transfer, the subsequent payment into the trust-controlled account, Malcolm's signed approval and the evidence behind the forged letter. It included his denial of financial wrongdoing and called for an independent review of the remaining awards. A separate, conspicuous correction withdrew the old suggestion that a personal quarrel explained Claire's disappearance. The newsroom protected the identities of applicants and did not describe Claire's private testimony as a court finding.

James read the correction. He told Emma that it could not restore the years the family had lost, but that withdrawing the headline mattered. He was not offering forgiveness, and she did not ask for it.

In the research log, the early anonymous contacts remained unattributed; Reid's acknowledged omission still called for an official response. The unresolved student cases, review procedures and missing totals belonged to the wider audit. Emma would not let a corrected headline imply that those separate questions had also been settled.

That night, back in her Edinburgh flat, Emma took Claire's first letter from the drawer where she had kept it. For fifteen years she had wanted a final sentence that explained everything: why Claire vanished, who benefited, where the money went. The surviving evidence could not honestly provide one.

But it had established something more enduring than a neat accusation. The second letter had been a deliberate attempt to silence questions. The first had asked Emma to ask better ones. And Claire, still alive, had chosen to answer in her own voice, without surrendering the right to remain out of sight.

Emma folded the paper along its original crease. This time, she had not made the last word hers.
